title: the best comment on my last AI trading post exposed a hole in "explainability"
author: CODE_HEIST
selftext:
a few days ago i posted about why an AI trading agent should explain every buy, rejection and rule change.

the most useful reply pointed out a gap i had not framed clearly.

versioning the strategy is not enough.

say an entry rule rejects tokens above 20% holder concentration. the config can stay identical while a data provider changes how concentration is calculated.

same rule. different input meaning. different decision.

so a useful decision receipt needs more than a model explanation:

\- strategy version and config hash

\- the exact input snapshot the agent saw

\- source and collection time

\- raw values before normalization

\- every check that passed or failed

\- intended action, submitted order and final outcome

without that, a replay can reconstruct what the system sees today instead of what it knew when the decision was made.

i'm thinking through this while building TrenchersAI. the goal is not to make a wrong trade sound intelligent. it is to make the wrong decision reproducible.

the attached screenshot is an exact TrenchersAI Paper-mode screen. it shows the configuration change log that exists today, not the complete decision-receipt architecture described above and not a live performance claim.

for people running agents live, what belongs in a minimum decision receipt that i'm still missing?

comments.author: leroylabs
comments.body:
For the 20% holder-concentration check, I'd add the provider's metric/schema version and your normalization code version. Raw values help, but replay also needs the definition used then, including which wallets were excluded. If the provider doesn't expose that definition, mark that part of the receipt as unverifiable.

Your Paper screenshot shows minimum holders changing from 30 to 150. Each check should record the observed value, effective threshold, and pass/fail/unknown status. A missing holder count shouldn't silently look like a failed threshold check. Could a receipt distinguish a provider timeout from an actual concentration rejection?
